blocks.prompt: The Bear With the Wrong Stomach
blocks.text: Almost every bear eats a little of everything. A brown bear will take fish from a river, dig up roots, raid a beehive, and finish with a mouthful of berries. The giant panda gave all of that up. It eats bamboo, and it eats almost nothing else. That choice is strange, because the panda still has the body of a meat eater. Its gut is short and simple, like a wolf's. It has no extra stomach for breaking down plants, the way a cow does. So the panda gets very little food out of every bite. It solves the problem by eating an enormous amount. A grown panda can eat forty pounds of bamboo in a day, and it spends ten to sixteen hours a day chewing. Holding bamboo takes a good grip. A panda has five fingers on each front paw, and none of them is a thumb. Instead it has a knob of bone in its wrist that sticks out and presses against the other fingers. It is not a real thumb. It works anyway.

blocks.prompt: The Bear With the Wrong Body for Its Job
blocks.text: The giant panda is a bear that behaves like a cow and is built like a wolf. All three of those things are true at once, and together they make the panda one of the strangest animals alive. Start with the food. Bamboo makes up about ninety-nine percent of a panda's diet. Bamboo is not a tree. It is a grass, and like most grasses it is mostly tough fiber with very little nourishment locked inside. Cows and deer handle food like this with long, complicated guts full of bacteria that spend days fermenting every mouthful. The panda has none of that. Its digestive system is short and simple, the standard equipment of a meat eater, inherited from bear ancestors who hunted. A panda pushes bamboo through that system in about half a day and absorbs roughly a sixth of it. The rest comes out the other end, sometimes forty times a day. The only fix is volume. An adult panda eats between twenty-six and eighty-four pounds of bamboo daily and spends ten to sixteen hours doing it. That leaves little time for anything else, which is why pandas look so unhurried. They cannot afford to hurry. Their bodies run on a famously low budget: one study found a panda burns energy at about a third of the rate expected for an animal its size, closer to a sloth than to a grizzly. Other bears sleep through winter. A panda cannot store enough fat to try, so it walks downhill to warmer slopes and keeps chewing. There is one more piece of mismatched equipment. Pandas have no thumb, but they need to grip bamboo stalks, so a small wrist bone grew outward until it could press against the paw like one. Biologists call it a false thumb. It is the panda making do.

blocks.prompt: Why a Bear Stopped Eating Meat
blocks.text: Somewhere around four million years ago, the ancestors of the giant panda quietly lost the ability to enjoy meat. The evidence is written in the panda's genes. Mammals detect the savory flavor of meat using a receptor built from a gene called T1R1. In pandas, that gene is broken. It is still there, sitting in the genome like an unplugged appliance, but the mutations that disabled it are estimated to be around four million years old, which lines up with the fossil evidence for when pandas turned toward bamboo. A panda can still eat meat and will occasionally scavenge it. It simply has no strong reason to want it. What it wanted instead was bamboo, and bamboo is a poor bargain. It is a grass: abundant, evergreen, defended by almost nothing, and available in enormous quantities in the cold mountain forests of central China. It is also mostly indigestible fiber. The panda never evolved the long fermenting gut that cows and deer use to unlock plant matter. It kept the short, simple digestive tract of a carnivore and simply pushes more material through it, absorbing perhaps seventeen percent of what it swallows. Everything else about the panda follows from that thin margin. It eats for ten to sixteen hours a day. Its organs, including its brain, liver, and kidneys, are small for its size, because organs are expensive to run. Its thyroid hormone signaling is damped by a mutation, which slows the whole body down. Measurements show a wild panda burning energy at close to sloth levels, roughly a third of what a bear its size should need. It does not hibernate, because it can never bank the fat. There is one more catch, and it is the dangerous one. Bamboo does something no other staple food does. A bamboo species will flower once, all at the same time, across an entire mountainside, and then the whole stand dies. Pandas used to walk to the next valley. Roads, farms, and towns have cut the forest into islands, and a panda that cannot walk out of a dying stand of bamboo has nowhere to go. China's answer has been to build the corridors back. More than sixty reserves now protect panda forest, and replanted strips of bamboo stitch isolated groups together. It has worked better than most people expected. In 2016 the giant panda was moved off the endangered list and reclassified as vulnerable, with a wild count near 1,864. That is not a rescue. It is a reprieve.

notes: The false thumb is the radial sesamoid, a wrist bone
Stephen Jay Gould wrote about it in 1980
A 6-million-year-old fossil relative already had one
It stays short because it also bears weight when walking
Meat-taste gene inactive for about 4 million years
Metabolism idles near sloth levels

blocks.prompt: The Panda's Thumb, and What It Proves
blocks.text: In 1980 the biologist Stephen Jay Gould wrote an essay about a bone in a panda's wrist, and he used it to make a point about how evolution actually works. The essay has outlived most of the science writing of its decade, because the bone deserves the attention. A giant panda spends ten to sixteen hours a day stripping leaves from bamboo stalks. That job needs a grip, and a grip needs an opposable thumb. The panda does not have one. Like every other bear, it has five fingers on each front paw, all pointing the same direction, none of them able to swing across and meet the others. Evolution could not simply hand the panda a thumb, because the panda's ancestors had already committed those five fingers to walking. So it improvised. A small bone in the wrist, called the radial sesamoid, grew outward and downward until it formed a padded knob that the panda can press bamboo against. It is not a finger. It has no real joints and it barely moves. It is a repurposed wrist bone doing a passable impression of a thumb. Gould's point was that this is exactly what you should expect. A designer starting fresh would have given the panda a proper thumb. Evolution cannot start fresh. It can only modify what is already there, and the awkwardness of the result is the evidence that no one planned it. Clumsy solutions, he argued, are better proof of evolution than elegant ones. The story has since gotten better. In 2022, researchers described a six-million-year-old fossil of an early panda relative with the same enlarged wrist bone already in place. The false thumb is ancient, older than the modern panda itself. The fossil also suggested why the bone never grew longer, a question that had puzzled people for decades: the same bone helps carry the animal's weight when it walks. Lengthen it and the panda grips better but limps. The false thumb is short because it is doing two jobs, and neither one is allowed to win. That tension runs through the whole animal. The panda is a carnivore by ancestry and by equipment, with the short gut of a bear, living on a grass it can barely digest. It absorbs about seventeen percent of what it eats and compensates by eating almost constantly. Its gene for tasting the savory flavor of meat went dead roughly four million years ago and has sat inert in the genome ever since. Its metabolism idles at close to sloth levels. It cannot hibernate, because there is no surplus to store. For a long time all of this was read as a species in trouble, an evolutionary dead end shuffling toward extinction with or without human help. That reading is wrong, and it matters that it is wrong. The panda held an enormous range across China and Southeast Asia for millions of years on this exact strategy. Bamboo is a spectacular resource: evergreen, abundant, defended by nothing, and ignored by almost every large competitor. A body that runs slowly enough to live on it is not a failure. It is a specialist that solved a hard problem cheaply. What went wrong was not the panda. Its habitat has been cut into fragments by roads, farms, and towns, and fragmentation is uniquely dangerous for an animal whose food dies on purpose. Bamboo flowers synchronously, whole stands at once, and then dies back and takes years to return. A panda in an unbroken forest walks to the next valley. A panda on an island waits. China's response, sixty-odd reserves and replanted corridors linking them, has done what most conservation programs do not. It has worked. The giant panda was moved from endangered to vulnerable in 2016. The animal built entirely out of compromises is still here, still holding its bamboo with a wrist bone, still getting away with it.
